questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a feature store in an ML system?
options: To store trained model weights
To centralize ML features for reuse across teams and ensure training-serving consistency
To store raw data before processing
To manage user authentication for ML services
questions.explanation: A feature store centralizes feature definitions and data, preventing duplicate feature engineering across teams. It also ensures the same feature computation logic is used in both training and serving, avoiding training-serving skew.

questions.question: What is the difference between online and batch model serving?
options: Online serving is for testing, batch serving is for production
Online serving returns real-time predictions per request; batch serving pre-computes predictions for large datasets offline
Online serving uses GPUs, batch serving uses CPUs
Online serving is more accurate than batch serving
questions.explanation: Online serving handles individual prediction requests in real-time (millisecond latency). Batch serving processes millions of items offline (e.g., nightly recommendation scores). Many systems use both: batch for precomputation and online for real-time personalization.

questions.question: Why is A/B testing important for ML model deployment?
options: It reduces model training time
It validates that the new model actually improves business metrics in production with real users
It compresses the model for faster inference
It encrypts model predictions for security
questions.explanation: Offline metrics (accuracy, AUC) do not always correlate with real-world impact. A/B testing routes live traffic to both old and new models, measuring actual business metrics (clicks, conversions, revenue) to determine if the new model is truly better.

questions.question: What is a vector database used for in ML systems?
options: Storing SQL queries for model training
Storing high-dimensional embeddings and performing fast approximate nearest neighbor search
Storing model training logs
Storing user passwords securely
questions.explanation: Vector databases store embedding vectors (dense numerical representations of items, text, images) and provide efficient similarity search. They power recommendation engines, semantic search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems.

questions.question: How does the HNSW algorithm achieve fast approximate nearest neighbor search?
options: By sorting all vectors in a linear array
By building a multi-layer navigable graph where upper layers enable coarse navigation and lower layers enable fine-grained search
By using hash tables to bucket similar vectors
By compressing vectors to reduce dimensionality
questions.explanation: HNSW builds a hierarchy of graphs. The top layer has few nodes for long-range jumps (like highway express lanes). Each lower layer adds more nodes for finer navigation. Search starts at the top and navigates down, achieving O(log N) query time.

questions.question: What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?
options: Data drift is a network issue; concept drift is a storage issue
Data drift is when input feature distributions change; concept drift is when the relationship between features and labels changes
Data drift affects training; concept drift affects serving
Data drift is gradual; concept drift is always sudden
questions.explanation: Data drift means the statistical properties of input features have shifted (e.g., users are now younger). Concept drift means the underlying mapping from features to labels has changed (e.g., what users consider 'good' content has evolved). Both degrade model performance.

questions.question: What is training-serving skew and why is it dangerous?
options: When the training data is too large for the serving hardware
When features are computed differently during training vs serving, causing silent prediction errors
When the model trains too slowly compared to serving speed
When training uses GPUs but serving uses CPUs
questions.explanation: Training-serving skew occurs when feature computation logic differs between training and inference. For example, training normalizes with population statistics but serving uses batch statistics. This causes subtle prediction errors that are hard to detect.

questions.question: What is the role of a model registry in an ML pipeline?
options: To register users who access the model
To version, store, and manage trained models with metadata, enabling reproducibility and rollback
To register domain names for model APIs
To count the number of predictions made
questions.explanation: A model registry stores trained models alongside their metadata (training data version, hyperparameters, metrics, lineage). It enables version comparison, staged promotion (dev -> staging -> production), and rollback to previous versions if issues arise.

questions.question: Why might HNSW trade recall for speed, and when is this acceptable?
options: HNSW always returns exact results with no trade-off
HNSW may miss some true nearest neighbors for dramatically faster search; this is acceptable when finding approximately similar items is sufficient (e.g., recommendations)
HNSW only works with low-dimensional data
HNSW requires the entire dataset to fit in memory with no trade-offs
questions.explanation: HNSW is an approximate algorithm — it navigates a graph and may not explore every possible path. For recommendations or semantic search, finding 95% of the true nearest neighbors in 1ms is far more practical than finding 100% in 10 seconds.

questions.question: Your recommendation model's click-through rate drops 5% every Monday morning and recovers by Tuesday. What is the most likely cause and how would you address it?
options: A bug in the serving infrastructure that occurs on Mondays
Temporal data drift — user behavior patterns differ on Mondays; add day-of-week as a feature or train separate models
The model is retraining every Monday and temporarily degraded
Monday network latency causes prediction timeouts
questions.explanation: Cyclical performance drops indicate temporal data drift. Users behave differently on Mondays (e.g., work vs weekend browsing patterns). Solutions include adding temporal features, training day-specific models, or using time-aware embeddings to capture weekly patterns.
